title: You have humiliated yourself in front of people
lede: You said the wrong name, sent the message to the wrong thread, fell over, mispronounced something in a presentation, cried in a meeting, or told a joke into total silence. It is still happening on your face.

blocks.text: You said the wrong name, sent the message to the wrong thread, fell over, mispronounced something in a presentation, cried in a meeting, or told a joke into total silence. It is still happening on your face.

items: People remember your reaction far longer than the event. This is the whole of the good news and it is genuinely reliable.
The audience overestimation effect is enormous: observers notice and retain a small fraction of what you believe they did.
Attempted concealment converts a five-second event into a story. The cover-up is always more memorable than the mistake.
Recovering well from something embarrassing raises your status rather than lowering it, because composure under exposure is rare and visible.

items.move: Name it lightly, once, and move on
items.detail: Four words maximum, then continue as if nothing happened. The moving on is the technique.
One acknowledgement. Repeated apology forces everyone to keep attending to it.

items.move: Fix the practical part immediately if there is one
items.detail: Unsend the message, correct the figure, send the right file. Practical repair, no drama.
Do not shrink, hide your face, or leave the room. Posture is what the room reads.

items.move: Say a real sentence to the person affected
items.detail: If someone was hurt or misnamed, address them directly and briefly, in private if possible.
Fleeing makes it the defining event of the day. Ordinary continuation dissolves it.

items.when: If you got a name wrong
items.say: "Sorry, Priya — I know your name, my brain just left. Anyway, your point about the timeline."
"That was meant for someone else and I am mortified. Ignore it and I will not do it again."
"I care about this more than I meant to show. Give me a minute and I will carry on."

items: Explaining at length why it happened. Nobody needs the backstory.
Making a running joke of it for the rest of the day. It keeps it alive.
Sending a long apology email an hour later about something trivial.
Avoiding the person or the room afterwards. Avoidance is what converts embarrassment into a lasting anxiety.
Replaying it that night. Write one line about what you would do differently and close the file.
Go back to the same room, the same people, the next day, and be normal. That is the actual repair.
If it was a genuine error, fix the system that allowed it — a different send delay, a checked name list, a rehearsal.
Notice in a week how little anyone mentions it. Collect that evidence deliberately; it is what recalibrates you.
Tell it as a funny story once you can. Ownership permanently removes its power.
